content:
Hello everyone,

I’ve started to formalize some basic results from the theory of clones (a set of functions that contains the projections and is closed under composition) in Lean. The goal is to learn more about Lean through a specific project, to formalize the Galois connection to constraint satisfaction problems (CSP), and eventually to write out the full result from Post (e.g. Post's_lattice) later. Suggestions on how to improve this are very welcome (see: Codeberg).
Nice to see the topic of my PhD. I was formalizing this every once a while but never too seriously. By the way, do you know that abstract clones are essentially monads, and abstract minions functors?

Post's lattice was also the subject of my PhD (complexity theory, classification of variants of SAT). Where can I find information about monads and minion functors? I've never heard of anything like that before. To me, it has always been an application of ("strange") universal algebra in the context of circuits.

I was in the topic of universal algebra -- looking at things much more from the perspective of clones, and the equations they satisfy rather than from computational complexity. Although the correspondence between clones & relational clones (pp-definitions) was also very essential to me. I learned that these are nothing else than monads later, but they indeed are... (just that is a language of category theorists, and not universal algebra)

Very roughly, a monad is "something like List" in the sense that there the following three operations:

map : A → B → List A → List B
singleton : A → List A
flatten : List (List A) → List A->

satisfying the following

-- map is a functor
map id = id -- id is the identity mapping x ↦
map (f ∘ g) = (map f) ∘ (map g)
-- "left & right unit"
flatten (singleton lst) = lst
flatten (map singleton lst) = lst
-- "associativity"
flatten (flatten lst3d) = flatten (map flatten lst3d)

Instead of map & flatten, people often use flattenMap as the basic operation (it is called bind in the language of monads), defined by

bind (lst : List A) (f : A → list B) : List B := flatten (map f lst)

satisfying

bind (singleton x) f = f x
bind lst singleton = lst
bind (bind lst f) g = bind lst (fun x ↦ bind (f x) g)

Clones

In the context of clones, a clone is basically a function

funcOfArity : I → Set ((I → domain) → domain)

which takes a finite indexing set I, and assigns all the functions in the clone with this indexing set. Alongside with this, you have

projection : A -> funcOfArity A
compose : funcOfArity A -> (A -> funcOfArity B) -> funcOfArity B

if you look at it, projection has exactly the type of singleton (in monads, this is usually called pure), compose has the same type of bind, and they satisfy the very same axioms.

Moreover, in universal algrebra, we also have a concept of abstract clones -- the idea is similar as with group theory: People were first studying groups as just "sets of permutations closed under compositions". Later they realized that the most important aspect of a group is not which specific permutations they represent, but only how the elements compose. You can do a similar abstraction with a clone -- remembering only labels for projections, and how elements compose without knowing which functions they are. This is essentially nothing else than an abstract monad with one little catch -- that monads usually operate on a single category, but clones usually have finite arity (so it is say the category of finite sets / finite types) and possibly infinite domain (so it is a category of sets / types). But maybe one could just allow infinite arity, and add an axiom that all functions are essentially finite?

I was thinking that if I for example wanted to get clone theory into Mathlib, I probably should link it to their monad theory because some of the basic simplification results (how to simplify composition...) is indeed the same, and already implemented. On the other hand, I was never really sure how it fits.

Minions

At some point, the research group in Prague (Libor Barto...) shifted focus from clones to minions because they found that minions essentially capture enough information about computational complexity, and are more basic than clones. Minions do really need projections nor compositions. The only operation that they must be closed upon is argument gluing & rearrangement. For example, you can define 3-ary g out of 4-ary f as follows.

g(a, b, c) = f(b,a,b,a)

This corresponds to the map function in the context of monads / lists, so it is essentially nothing but just a functor.

Just a topic to think about...
